title: Content Safety and Guardrails
description: Apply safety filtering, input validation, and output guardrails to AI-backed .NET endpoints.

blocks.text: AI features need guardrails at multiple layers: input validation, retrieved context filtering, output moderation, and operational limits. In .NET backends, these layers can be implemented as middleware, decorators, or separate services.

blocks.title: Where to apply safety controls
items: **Input filters** — block or log suspicious prompts before retrieval or generation.
**Context filters** — reject retrieved chunks that violate policy or security rules.
**Output moderation** — scan LLM responses before returning them to users.
**Operational limits** — rate limits, token budgets, and fallback behavior.

blocks.title: Assume prompts are untrusted
blocks.text: Never trust user input or retrieved documents. Both can contain prompt injection attempts designed to bypass instructions.

items.text: I can identify guardrail layers in my backend
items.hint: Input filters, context filters, output moderation, operational limits

items.text: I know how to use Azure Content Safety in .NET
items.hint: Call the Content Safety API from a service or middleware

items.text: I have a fallback plan for unsafe responses
items.hint: Return a safe default message and log the event

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Safety must be enforced at input, retrieval, and output layers.
Content filtering and guardrails reduce legal and reputational risk.
Failures should produce safe defaults, not unmoderated responses.
blocks.takeaway: Build safety in from the start. Retrofit guardrails are brittle and often miss edge cases.
